# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-21 (Extended v152)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (spring Year 6)**: Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house with secret passage to Rue de Babylone), Place de la Bastille (elephant monument under construction), Prison Charlemagne (Fine-Air top story), Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile (ruin wall), Dunstead harbor town (English provincial setting). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 (frost, rain, thunder, muddy roads, early darkness) transitioned to spring Year 6 (described as "spring of the sixth year"). Provincial English towns: Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided to Luvie Prydenridge that fire at Dunstead granary was set on purpose—unverified.

## Primary Locations
**RUE PLUMET HOUSE**: Single-story pavilion in deserted Rue Plumet with approximately one-and-a-half-acre garden. Two ground-floor rooms, two first-floor chambers, downstairs kitchen, upstairs boudoir, attic. Secret-spring door masked in rear building communicates via long narrow paved corridor to Rue de Babylone quarter-league distant.

**PLACE DE LA BASTILLE ELEPHANT MONUMENT**: Rough model forty feet high, constructed of timber and masonry, bearing tower. Enveloped in immense woodwork shirt. Interior accessed via black hole in belly: vast hollow space with long brown beam forming vertebral column, massive arching ribs, plaster stalactites, vast spider webs. **Rats swarming by thousands—frightened by voices but return when silent.** Large crack in roof where flue enters provides easy access point.

**PRISON CHARLEMAGNE (FINE-AIR TOP STORY)**: Large hall with Mansard roof, guarded with triple gratings and double doors of sheet iron. Four square cages separated by narrow passages, built to elbow height with iron bars to roof. Lighted by skylight. Sentry relieved every two hours with loaded musket. Jailer escorted by two dogs enters daily at four o'clock. Prisoners wear fetters weighing fifty pounds. Massive chimney-flue traverses all stories from ground floor kitchen, pierces roof.

**RUE DES BALLETS/RUE DU ROI-DE-SICILE RUIN**: Back wall of masonry rising to third-story height. Stark escarpment three stories high separates ruin edge from pavement below. Rotten plank fence with gate fastened only by latch. Little shanty leans against ruin remnant.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (Autumn Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn (origin unclear). Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself entirely to his care.

**Recovery and charitable work**: Convalesced through March-April. Resumed carrying bread to hungry, clothing to cold. Cosette often accompanied him.

**Mysterious journeys**: Valjean took occasional journeys of one or two days, destination unknown to Cosette. Pattern: typically when money lacking in house.

**Nocturnal garden activity and manuscript**: Cosette observed figure walking in garden dusk carrying large club. Found stone on bench; became alarmed, closed shutters. Later discovered packet of philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark, immortal, incorruptible, infinite. **Cosette recognized writer as Marius.**

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (Autumn Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never truly forgotten Marius, had always loved and adored him. "The fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it had burst forth afresh, and had inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter (autumn Year 5)**: Marius grasped Cosette in garden as she fell. They fell upon bench; their lips met without knowing how. Serene, splendid night overhead. "Effusion followed silence, which is fulness." Two beings "pure as spirits" confided everything—dreams, intoxications, ecstasies, longings, despair. "Their two hearts poured themselves out into each other in such wise, that at the expiration of a quarter of an hour, it was the young man who had the young girl's soul, and the young girl who had the young man's soul."

**Marius's nightly visits (spring Year 6)**: Beginning with kiss that betrothed their souls, Marius came every evening. Éponine had recognized Valjean's house, kept ruffians away from Rue Plumet, then conducted Marius there. Marius entered garden by forcing old gate's decrepit bars; being slender, readily passed through. **Authorial reflection on danger**: "One of woman's magnanimities is to yield. Love, at the height where it is absolute, is complicated with some indescribably celestial blindness of modesty. But what dangers you run, O noble souls!" Love is "life, if it is not death. Cradle; also coffin." The human heart sheds "the most light, alas! and the most darkness."

## Thénardiers and Child Substitution
**Family disruption**: Thénardiers imprisoned following Jondrette garret arrest.

**Magnon arrangement**: Before police raid, Thénardier handed two little sons to Magnon (fashionable woman in criminal sphere) with intention of renouncing them forever. Magnon promised ten francs monthly, actually paid. M. Gillenormand (grandfather) continued compact, visiting every six months without perceiving change. Children well cared for, better treated by false mother than real mother.

**Spring 1832 dispersal**: Shortly after Magnon handed note to Éponine, police raid made in Rue Clocheperce. Magnon and Mamselle Miss (English thief, naturalized Parisienne) seized; house emptied. **Two children set out alone, elder leading younger, holding paper with address M. Barge, collector of rents, Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, No. 8. Gust of wind tore paper from elder's fingers; unable to find it again as night fell. Lost in city, wandering in spring cold.**

## Gavroche and the Two Lost Children (Spring 1832—Spring Year 6)
**Gavroche's character**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Stole Montparnasse's purse (late April Year 5). "Always shivering gayly under his rags." Engages in "shaving barbers"—stealing soap cakes to sell to hair-dressers in suburbs.

**Encounter and rescue (spring 1832)**: While scrutinizing wig-maker's shop near Orme-Saint-Gervais, observed two neatly dressed children of unequal stature. Barber thrust them back furiously. Gavroche provided bread and promised shelter.

**Elephant shelter (spring 1832—spring Year 6)**: Led two children through fence gap into elephant enclosure. Climbed to black hole in belly. Elder undertook climb; younger felt inclined to cry but did not dare. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5. **Winter Year 5 nocturnal incident**: Five-year-old heard hubbub overhead, jogged elder brother's elbow. Younger questioned Gavroche in low tone. **Gavroche grasped little fellow's hand across his brother; child felt reassured. Courage and strength communicated mysteriously. All three fell fast asleep during wintry gale and rain.**

## Prison Escape: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, Montparnasse, and Thénardier (Winter Year 5, Early Morning—4 a.m. to Dawn)
**Thénardier's confinement**: Rated as burglar, detained in Fine-Air cage since night of 3d February under charge of organizing nocturnal ambush with armed force. Kept on feet with fifty-pound fetters. Obtained permission to keep iron bolt "to preserve bread from rats." Procured and secreted bottle of wine with narcotic invented by Desrues, rendered famous by _Endormeurs_ (Sleep-compellers).

**Brujon and Guelemer's escape**: When Gavroche picked up two lost children, Brujon and Guelemer rose softly and with nail began piercing chimney against which their beds stood. Showers mingled with thunder created opportune uproar. Before sound reached watcher, wall pierced, chimney scaled, grating forced. Two ruffians reached roof, fastened rope to iron bar stumps, crossed six-foot abyss eighty feet above ground to surrounding wall, descended to bath-house courtyard, traversed it, pushed porter's wicket, pulled rope, opened porte-cochère, found themselves in street. **Successfully escaped.**

**Thénardier's escape and stranding**: At two o'clock morning, old sentinel relieved by conscript. Hours later, man with dogs paid visit, went off without noticing except possibly recruits's youth and "rustic air." At four o'clock, relieving sentinel found conscript asleep near Thénardier's cage. **Thénardier vanished. Hole in cage ceiling and above in roof. One bed plank wrenched off. Half-empty bottle with stupefying wine seized. Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** Thénardier, dripping with perspiration, drenched with rain, clothes hanging in ribbons, hands flayed, elbows bleeding, knees torn, reached edge of ruin wall at Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile. **Stretched at full length; strength failed him. Separated from street pavement three stories below by steep escarpment.**

**Four ruffians' vigil and rescue attempt**: Four o'clock struck. Terrified uproar burst forth in prison—doors opening, gratings creaking, lights ascending and descending, torches running along ridge-poles, firemen summoned. **Thénardier perceived wan whiteness at Bastille edge lighting sky in doleful wise—dawn arriving. Pale, exhausted, desperate, hidden by night but knowing day was dawning, alarmed sentinel would be found asleep within minutes.** Staring at terrible depth, at wet black pavement—longed for yet frightful, meaning both death and liberty.

**Four ruffians' vigil and Gavroche's involvement**: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, and Montparnasse prowled all night around La Force hoping to see Thénardier appear on wall. Night growing too fine, downpour rendered streets deserted, cold overpowering them, alarming prison noise erupted, patrol encountered, hope vanishing. **Montparnasse himself, perhaps almost Thénardier's son-in-law, yielded. Moment more and they would be gone.** **Thénardier panting like shipwrecked sufferers when vessel vanished on horizon.** **Guelemer seized Gavroche by one arm, set him on roof of shanty, handed him rope knotted by Brujon. Gavroche directed steps towards flue—easy to enter thanks to large crack touching roof. At moment on point of ascending, Thénardier bent over wall edge; first light of dawn struck white upon his sweat-dripping brow, livid cheek-bones, sharp nose, bristling gray beard. Gavroche recognized him.**

**Gavroche's transformation**: As soon as Gavroche touched pavement, out of danger, he was no longer weary, chilled, or trembling. Terrible things vanished like smoke. "Strange and ferocious mind awoke once more, stood erect and free, ready to march onward."

## Authorial Digressions on Progress, History, and Social Danger (Chapters 20-21)
**Past versus Progress**: "The past is very strong, it is true, at the present moment. It censures...This dead body is a conqueror...He advances, he threatens, he laughs, he is at our doors. Let us not despair, on our side. Let us sell the field on which Hannibal is encamped."

**Progress and the future**: "When they say 'no' to progress, it is not the future but themselves that they are condemning...There is but one way of rejecting To-morrow, and that is to die."

**Social philosophy and equilibrium**: "Immense combined propulsions direct human affairs...to a state of equilibrium; that is to say, to equity...This force is a worker of miracles...we may expect anything from that mysterious power of progress."

**Social phthisis and remedy**: Thanks to Revolution, old feudal/monarchical maladies no longer run in blood. No more Jacquerie. Apoplexy feared no longer, but society must heed how it breathes. **"Social phthisis called misery."** Intellectual and moral growth indispensable as material improvement. "To know is sacrament, think is prime necessity, truth is nourishment as well as grain. Reason fasting from science grows thin."

**Ideal persisting despite darkness**: "The ideal is frightful to behold, thus lost in the depths, small, isolated, imperceptible, brilliant, but surrounded by those great, black menaces, monstrously heaped around it; yet no more in danger than a star in the maw of the clouds."

**Conclusion on human imperishability**: "Beneath the social mortality, we feel human imperishableness. The globe does not perish, because it has these wounds...The maladies of the people do not kill man."

## Provincial Characters (Winter Year 5—Spring Year 6)
Vesmira, Luvie Prydenridge, Isvie Stenworth, Marald Corrford, Fenelle Lindmere, Elra Corrford, Bremira, Yedan Corrford, Ferald Stenworth, Thizek, Thizek Stenenridge, Lura. **Late night rumor/claim**: Fenelle Lindmere confided to youngest son of Yedan Corrford that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified. Miscellaneous provincial details: Cart with turnips, baker's boy late, oven line, coin shortages, weather predictions, almanac readings, vespers bells, salt-tar wind smell, gulls over fish heads, bees in lavender, flat smoke over fields, bone compass sent by carrier.
